We are thinking along the same lines.
This worries me.

By having observer status for a while we could see what problems we might encounter if we became a full member, and we would have better grounds upon which to decide whether we should or should not join. I certainly look forward to the minister's observations later in this debate.
Before sitting down there is one other thing I would like to mention, and that is Canada's relationship with the West Indies and the Caribbean. Every effort should be made to increase our close association with these countries, and in particular I would mention one which is shortly to become independent, British Guiana. Our colleagues in the United Kingdom are faced with great difficulties at the present time. Their armed forces are spread very thinly through the trouble spots in Yemen, Cyprus, South Arabia, and the like. It is also a well known fact that there might well be trouble in British Guiana, and it is my understanding that the United Kingdom has very skimpy forces there at present, which causes the United Kingdom great concern.
It might be helpful in this area if the minister gave consideration to offering the use of certain Canadian forces in this very important area of the Caribbean. It is getting pretty close to home. It is not too far from

Supply-External Affairs Cuba, and I do not think I need say more or elaborate in this regard at this time. It is something the government should consider.
Again I want to thank the committee for allowing me the extended period of time in which to make my remarks, and at this point I will now sit down.

Mr. Chairman, I would very much like to open my remarks by welcoming the review of foreign policy given us this morning by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. With a very great deal of what he said I imagine no reasonable Canadian of good will could possibly disagree, but there are some points of difference of opinion which I would like to mention, and some differences of emphasis I would like to discuss in the course of my remarks.
I imagine, Mr. Chairman, all members of the committee have received a very beautifully edited magazine about the President of the United States. In it was an article on the late President Kennedy, written by Arthur Schlesinger Jr., who was his special assistant. In it he used these words with which I would like to preface my remarks:
Every significant statesman must possess and be possessed by a vision of the future. He must have some instinct about the grand movement of history, and must perceive some direction in which he supposes the world is moving. He must have a conception of the historical process which connects what has been and what is to come, and which therefore gives his present deeds and decisions a setting and a point. Implanted within him there must be an image, not necessarily conscious or explicit, but plastic and capacious of the world he strives to bring into being.
I imagine it would be difficult, in fact presumptuous, for all of us to seek to be significant statesmen; nevertheless I think it would be worth while for us, in making our comments in this discussion on external affairs and on the statement given to us by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to set them in the context of our understanding of the world situation today and in the light of some sort of vision of the world of the future. I would say, Mr. Chairman, that the significant feature of today's world is its radically changing nature. There are today new opportunities, and there are new threats. If one's thinking is clear it seems to me that it would not be good enough for us to go on meeting these new threats with the methods that were appropriate to meet the old. If we do not seize the new opportunities we may lose them and they will never recur. These remarks, I think, are appropriate in discussing our position in international affairs.
When he spoke to the special committee on defence in July last, the Secretary of State

for External Affairs stated that the foreign and) defence policies of any state in the nuclear age are inseparable, and they must both have but a single objective, the preservation of peace. With that statement I most heartily concur.
If I may mention a personal matter I had the privilege, as did some other hon. members, of having lunch today with Dr. Matsumoto from Japan, who was a school teacher in Hiroshima at the time of the explosion of the nuclear bomb. He lost his wife, and 378 of the girl students died. He is here on a mission to try to explain that experience to other people in the world. With that experience in mind, I am sure none of us will disagree with the proposition that the-major objective of both foreign and defence policy-which, as the minister said, are inseparable-must be the preservation of peace. In that light I want to look at NATO, which the Secretary of State for External Affairs discussed with us this morning.
It was created in 1949 under conditions totally different from those which prevail at present. It was created to meet the threat of Soviet aggression in Europe, but uniting the nations of Europe in an alliance which was backed up by the United States nuclear monopoly. Without that backing, the nations of western Europe might well have fallen victims either to the internal subversion or external military threat of Soviet conventional power. But the situation has radically changed since that time. The western European nations have recovered their economic strength. In the common market and other western European institutions, they have recovered a sense of strength and independence, and in addition the world has entered a new era. It is the era of the hydrogen bomb, the era of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The United States of America no longer has the nuclear monopoly. We have reached a situation, it seems to me and to many people, of a nuclear stalemate, and at the present time we have in Europe massive confrontation of tactical nuclear weapons equal, as Mr. McNamara has told us, to 10,000 Hiro-shimas and Nagasakis put together. From this I think we can deduce that any major conflict in Europe would quickly escalate into all-out nuclear war. Fortunately it is clear that Mr. Khrushchev and his advisers are well aware of this. Indeed we know that this was one of the main items in the dispute which shattered the myth of communist unity and put the U.S.S.R. and the peoples of the republic of China into open conflict. In these circumstances no one who is not crazy

would risk a major conflict in Europe, and no one believes that the leaders of the U.S.S.R. are crazy.
There remains nevertheless a danger of war, a danger that we set off war by accident or by the impelling incentive in case of tension to strike first before you are struck. I suggest that it is on minimizing and reducing these risks that the major emphasis should be put both in NATO and in the disarmament conferences that are taking place at Geneva. But, Mr. Chairman, apart from this threat of accidental war or war induced, as I say, by the dangerous nature of the weapons which we possess in superabundance, we can, I think, reasonably look forward to a period of relative stability, a period in which the two major powers of the world have a strong, common interest in co-existence. The threat which NATO was designed to meet has been lessened by these facts and we would be foolish in my judgment to put our major emphasis in international affairs into meeting a waning and almost non-existent threat. We are aware that on both sides of the iron curtain there is no longer a monolithic picture. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that we should not be speaking of the east versus the west. On both sides of the iron curtain he agrees that there are indications of various sorts of a changed picture. There is no longer monolithic unity on either side. Therefore we have a period of relative stability based upon this balance of nuclear power.
My belief is that we must use the time bought by this measure of stability through the nuclear stalemate in order to create institutions on an international basis which will put on a far firmer foundation than any balance of mutual terror possibly can the hopes for peace of the world. If we say that we have acquired a degree of stability in Europe because of this nuclear confrontation, we must simultaneously admit that other developments throughout the world are creating major areas of instability, and I suggest it is to these major revolutionary movements in other parts of the world that our chief attention should be directed at the present time.
These major revolutionary developments involve not only the technological changes that have brought us all together so that we now discuss, as the minister has said, the affairs of Viet Nam, the affairs of Cyprus, affairs in every quarter of the world. There is also the major development of political emancipation, and I think that a basic fact that we sometimes overlook and which creates insta-
Supply-External Affairs bility is the tremendous disparity in living standards between the peoples of two thirds of the world and the peoples in other parts of the world. So, Mr. Chairman, I think it is to this type of threat to stability that we should be devoting more attention.
I suggest that Canada must remain within the NATO alliance, but I welcome what I understood to be the statement of the minister, that he believes that concrete new developments for more effective consultation within NATO are required. I was sorry that he was not able to tell us that any of these concrete solutions were either suggested at the council meeting he attended or that he himself has any in mind with regard to the development of NATO.
But I think that more important than the maintenance of these regional alliances at the present time is the meeting of this other threat which can only be met if we build up the world institution; in other words, it can be met only if we turn the United Nations, so far as we are able to do so, into a power, in embryo if you like, that can create something of the nature of a world government eventually, but in the meantime at any rate can be a force working for peace in all of these unstable areas of the world. Whether or not we recognize it, we have to build in this generation a world community, or we have to perish.
What does this mean in terms of concrete policy today? I suggest it means putting our major emphasis on the development of the United Nations. It is for that reason that we in this section of the house warmly welcomed the intervention, in which I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs gave great leadership, of the United Nations in Cyprus. We are disturbed by some of the details there, but any disturbance we may have is entirely secondary to our earnest desire to see this new experiment which is being carried on now in different parts of the world gain experience-gain, moreover, the experience which will enable it to be done more effectively in the future.
We cannot expect 100 per cent success, as I think the hon. member for Oxford suggested, in these first efforts. I welcome, and we in this part of the house all welcome the intervention of our forces in Cyprus, difficult, painful and perhaps even unsuccessful as it could possibly be in the long run. We cannot weigh things by whether they are 100 per cent successful at the time or whether they are easy. We have to do what we can, and we

Supply-External Affairs commend the part played by the government in carrying through this experiment.
As one who, as some members know, has been interested in law, I am reminded that the common law of Britain, which is regarded as quite an achievement of civilization, was not laid down by any prior plan but gradually broadened out from precedent to precedent, and I suspect that the development of the peace keeping powers of the United Nations will come about in somewhat the same way.
For the same reason we warmly welcome the initiative which has been taken by the government in planning to create stand-by forces for the United Nations. I had intended to read into the record certain remarks made by the Prime Minister in an article in Maclean's magazine of May 2 last. Perhaps I should read one or two sentences from it because in what he says he has the warm concurrence of the members of this group. He is dealing with the need for leadership to bring this about, for a constructive initiative toward peace and security by establishing stand-by forces. He said:
There must be leadership to bring this about- As a leading middle power, with a well known record of support for United Nations peace keeping operations in widely spread theatres, Canada is in a unique position to take the initiative. It is prepared to do so. It is anxious to develop its close co-operation with other U.N. members in these vital endeavours; to explore with them means for strengthening the United Nations' capacity to act in this field and the ability of member states to participate.
To that statement we here say "amen", and we hope that not only will this policy be carried out but that our defence dispositions will clearly be made in a way that will enable us to carry out the obligations that are to be assumed in this way. I say quite frankly, that simply is not the situation now and I have serious doubts whether the white paper will permit us to do that and carry out the other obligations referred to there. However, I do not want to digress too far into matters that relate strictly to defence, although they are closely interrelated.
There is another activity under NATO about which I feel far less happy. I am going to read to the house the answer to a question I put on the order paper. I realize that what was done was not done during the administration of the present government, but I should like to ask the minister to inquire about this matter because I find it disquieting. I read in a newspaper, the Montreal Gazette, I believe-I do not have it with me-that

Canada had some sort of joint arrangement of mutual aid under NATO whereby we and the United States jointly were to supply 120 F-104G aircraft, to be assembled by Cana-dair in Montreal, to Greece and Turkey as part of the mutual aid program. I was naturally interested in this when, at the present time, there is some real danger of conflict between these two allies of ours in NATO. I, therefore, put a question on the order paper and was given the following information as recorded at page 3213 of Hansard for May 13, 1964:
On June 12, 1961, Canada and the United States concluded an agreement under which F-104G aircraft, support equipment and spares to the value of U.S. $200 million were to be produced in Canada. Of the total cost, the U.S. government was to pay $150 million and the Canadian government $50 million. It was agreed that the aircraft produced under this arrangement would be used to meet Canadian mutual aid contributions to NATO and U.S. military assistance program requirements. According to most recent estimates, it is expected that this sum will cover the production of approximately 140 aircraft; the figure of 120 was an earlier estimate. Delivery of aircraft from the production line is still in its early stages, and it is not expected that production will be completed until October, 1965.
Then, I call attention to this statement:
In late 1961, the Canadian government agreed that title to all aircraft produced under this program should be vested in the United States. An understanding was reached whereby the U.S., having title, would decide the allocation of the aircraft, taking into account Canadian views.
This seems to me to be a very extraordinary statement, Mr. Chairman, that we should put up $50 million-and we do not have too many bundles of $50 million-to purchase aircraft, and then vest title and the real disposition of the aircraft in the United States. I do not say this out of any lack of confidence in our allies but sometimes, under the guise of mutual aid as approved by congress, things are done which this parliament might well not approve. I suggest this is an arrangement which requires to be looked into carefully. I continue quoting:
Arrangements have since been made for the total production to be divided into two categories; aircraft purchased in Canada for the United States military assistance program, and aircraft produced for presentation to NATO countries as a joint Canada-United States program of assistance to NATO countries. Such aircraft as have been delivered to date all fall into the former category.
So far we have delivered aircraft which, I understand, were for the United States for disposition by them.
No decision has as yet been taken concerning the countries which will receive F-104G aircraft under a joint Canada-United States program of assistance to NATO countries.

Then, I had asked about specifications, but I was told that the technical specifications of these aircraft were classified military information. Although 1 am no expert on the fine points of defence I have, as a member of the defence committee, learned enough to know that this F-104G has a range of 400 miles and when acquired by Canada as Starfighters or CF-104's they were equipped solely with tactical nuclear arms. This may not be so with these particular machines. This does not seem to be the time to be arranging to deliver to Greece and Turkey these highly offensive weapons. I wonder if there is not a little inconsistency between this type of arrangement and what our soldiers are trying to do in Cyprus at the present time.
Then, the answer concludes in this way:
In the event that it is decided to allocate to Greece and Turkey any of the aircraft produced under the latter program, the normal conditions attached to Canadian mutual aid will apply, viz., that recipient countries will use any material they receive to strengthen the capacity of NATO to deter or resist aggression.
But, Mr. Chairman, in the possession of nations at war, whose existence is at stake, are these conditions likely to be very meaningful? As I said, these arrangements appear to have been made some time before the present administration came into power, but the eventual disposition does not seem to have been decided. I should like to know what the answer is to a proposition whereby we put up $50 million of our money and provide that control of these offensive weapons is in the United States. The control is in the United States and apparently the eventual disposition of these is in the United States. This phrase is reminiscent of the Columbia treaty. As the minister will recall, the phrase in that treaty was that they would take into account Canadian views-and then make their own decision.
There was another aspect of the speech by the Secretary of State for External Affairs which I found, I must say, partly exasperating and partly delightful because it was so well done. This was the part in which the minister discussed our relations with the people's republic of China and it was, I would say, a typical and very skilful performance. Once again he gave us, as clearly as could be, good major reasons why we should not continue the isolation of the republic of China. He then proposed an exchange of journalists, and I have no objection to this proposition at all. It is delightful that we should learn something about what goes on in one quarter of the globe. If the journalists from China can find anything in Canada
Supply-External Affairs that would interest their readers, personally I would be delighted that they should do so.
The minister reminded me of a gentleman in early spring in a bathing suit, going out shivering, putting his toe in the water and getting ready to dive in, then his courage leaves him and he puts on his dressing gown and retires to sit in front of the fire once again, and saying, "Some time in the future". The logical consequence of what he said would have required him to finish with an announcement that we were exchanging diplomatic representatives with the People's Republic of China, and that we would, under proper conditions, support the admission of the de facto government of that country into the United Nations. In this connection, I noticed a statement the Prime Minister made when he was in Paris, and I think the minister was with him at that time. He said this:
Two courses are open to us. One Is the diplomatic and economic ostracism and isolation of states behind the iron curtain.
I ask you to note those words:
One is the diplomatic and economic ostracism and isolation of states behind the iron curtain. This course, Canada rejects.
If we reject it, why do we not do something about it? I know there are complications and difficulties, but if Mr. de Gaulle can recognize the People's Republic of China, then so can we. The minister discussed the matter with him and told us he agreed with many of the reasons that impelled that decision. This suggests that it is about time we carried out the logical consequences of what the minister has said when he referred to the continuing isolation of the de facto government of a quarter of the people of the world.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
In view of what the hon. member has said, what does he propose to do about the Formosan government?

I think there is not the slightest doubt that conditions should be attached to any admission of the People's Republic of China to the United Nations, that the Formosans should be given the right to choose, by referendum or otherwise, what form of government they prefer. I think that should be clearly recognized. We do have to get into a two-China policy. I do not think it would be right or proper for us to say we will just hand over that country, which is independent, to the people's republic of China. We do not

Supply-External Affairs yet know, at least 1 do not believe we know, whether, faced with the possibility of admission to the United Nations, that term might somehow or other be acceptable to the People's Republic of China.
The minister said conditions would be required. But you do not reach the stage of discussing conditions until you make up your mind that, subject to the conditions being met, you are ready to move. My criticism is that we have dilly-dallied too long on this subject. We in Canada are in a position, it seems to me, to use with other people in the world the interval which we believe exists to promote a world community.
I want to end my remarks by expressing a mild degree of disappointment that the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not find the question of external aid one which he thought necessary to review or emphasize, though he did mention the subject. I say this because it is my conviction that in building a world community we must have regard for the welfare of two thirds of the people of the world. We have a measure of responsibility. This has been requested by the United Nations, which we say we are trying to serve and build. The government has moved forward but, in my view, it has not moved forward as fast or as far as its own commitments require it to do. I have here a copy of a decision reached by the United Nations general assembly in 1961 to the effect that the standard contribution from the developed nations in economic aid should amount to 1 per cent of the income of those countries. That is not a very high standard. However, it was not chosen arbitrarily. The figure was set after careful examination.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am
sorry to say that the hon. member's time is a little more than expired.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The committee was very generous to me, and we agreed that the spokesman for the official opposition should extend his remarks. I would be happy to do that in this case.
Agreed.

I thought I heard someone say that the agreement was not without limit. I hasten to reassure the committee that I shall conclude my remarks in a very few minutes. I had reached the last point I wished to make, which is that the percentage figure for contributions to underdeveloped nations set by the United Nations assembly
[Mr. Brewin.)
itself was 1 per cent of the national income. In my view, this is not enough, but the figure is related to projects which could now be undertaken to meet the impact of this terrible problem caused by abject poverty in large sections of the world, a poverty which I suggest is one of the main causes of instability in the world today. Our own contribution has not risen above $100 million a year; I think the figure in the estimates for next year is of the order of $100 million. If we were to give the 1 per cent, we should be contributing $370 million. I do not think that less than half of the international standard suggested is good enough for a country which aspires, as Canada does, to leadership in the development of a world community, and I urge that this matter be given more attention by the government than it has in the past. Hon. gentlemen opposite have moved in the right direction. Their intentions are good. I do not think they need be frightened about what the people of Canada may think in this regard. When we are spending one and a half billion dollars on defence, surely we could spend more than we are now spending on this other aspect of the battle for the peace of the world.
I hope, also, we shall make a contribution on a far larger scale to research into those things which are required to bring about peace. We are spending plenty of money on research into so-called defence. We have the scientists, capable people, in Canada who could do this most important job in co-operation with other nations, and I hope the government will set about this task with the assistance of such organizations as the Canadian peace research institute. In his eloquent peroration the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the fact that Canada was not a major power and, therefore, did not have-I am paraphrasing his words -the awful responsibility which rested upon a major power. But, he went on to say, Canada does have a special responsibility-and I think I speak for all members of this party when I say I could not agree more. One of the reasons for this special responsibility is that we are not a major power. We welcome the initiative which the government has taken to strengthen the United Nations and to build up forces to support it. We hope they will go further and faster along that road because along that road, rather than in the maintenance of military alliances which are becoming obsolete, lies the hope of the world for peace in the future.

First, I should like to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs upon the effort and the thought which he put into his statement to this chamber this morning. I believe he attempted to give us a realistic review of world affairs as they stand at the present time. Certainly, what he had to say represented a great improvement over what we have been offered in the last year or so, as far as a realistic approach to world problems is concerned.
The minister said we had come a long way in Canada in the field of external affairs. He reminded us that 25 years ago it was difficult to get a government statement on foreign affairs. I agree that the situation has improved very much, but I think we still have a long way to go. I was disappointed to find this morning that we were fewer than 45 members in the house; the front benches on the government side were practically empty at the outset of what should be one of the most important occasions on which government policy is stated.
The minister began by saying that the world situation could no longer be divided on an east-west basis. He said the east-west label was no longer applicable and that he would like a better one. So he tried to find a more descriptive terminology. I think it does not matter what we call it; the world is still split in half. If the minister would like a better name, perhaps he should describe it as a fight between freedom and totalitarianism. The minister divided the world scene into four groups. He mentioned the free world and Russian communism as opposed to the Chinese type of communism. Then he spoke of the underdeveloped or uncommitted nations. I believe such a method of division covers up the fact that we are still divided into two camps, both of which are wooing the uncommitted nations. The side which will be most successful will be the one which is able to win the uncommitted nations to its camp. In my opinion the present phase of this struggle is far more dangerous than was the situation in the time of Stalin, when the war was fought out front and when the western nations were more or less driven to unite in face of a danger they could see.
Today the situation is much more deceiving; in fact, it is covered over in such a way that it is often difficult to determine and fully understand. It is much more subtle. If the minister really wants to differentiate between the Soviet type of communism and
Supply-External Affairs the Chinese type of communism, I think it would be wiser to do it in terms of strategy rather than in terms of their present attitudes toward the west, because I think both brands of communism have the same ultimate goal. Their only fight today, the only basis of their argument, is how best can they achieve that goal. Khrushchev is selling a soft line. By doing so I believe he has deadened the perceptive powers of the west; he deceives us into passiveness and often into lowering our guard. Mao Tse-tung, however uses the cold, brutal methods that Stalin used. These are often more impressive to the underdeveloped nations. Perhaps one of the reasons for this is that China is closer to them in their economic underdevelopment than is Russia herself.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, Khrushchev has adopted the method which he believes will succeed, and I think in many cases he is succeeding where Stalin's method failed. Stalin, in taking over much of eastern Europe, was unable to legalize or to gain any degree of acceptance for his takeover of those various countries. Khrushchev today, using the line that he is, is coming much closer to it. When he reaches the point where he is able to convince the people who live in these satellite nations that the west have forgotten about them, he will have accomplished his purpose. I believe that as he realistically looks at the world he understands the truth of the atomic situation relating to military force, because he knows he could not survive any more than could his enemies. So of necessity he is using this soft sell approach in talking to the rest of the world.
But again I would say that the communist approach is different only in strategy; their goals are the same. Whether you read a speech that comes out of Peking, or whether you read a speech that comes out of Moscow, every time a statement is made one should note that it defines their ultimate objective to be the takeover of the world for the communist way of life.
Therefore I think we must face up to this situation. We must face it as the grim reality that it is. Any attempt to rationalize these things will only mean we will be deceiving ourselves, and our efforts to promote those things in which we believe and which are the only alternative to this situation, I am convinced, will end in failure. How can the free world, in any permanent or substantive way, compete with the communist world, when the advantages are on their side? We are a free society. They can have their own political parties in our midst, as they have

Supply-External Affairs in the free countries of the world, and at any time they wish, they can flood those countries with propaganda. Can the free world do this in the other direction? It cannot. Therefore it seems to me that the only realistic approach to the many problems which face us in the world today is to face up to them.
I believe the minister, in trying to lay a new foundation for the policy which he has developed, is forgetting, or perhaps is attempting to rationalize the trade policies of the present government; because today the war that continues in the world has shifted from a military to an economic one; it is a cold war. I think the turning point was Cuba, because there we saw Khrushchev backing down to the threat of armed force, which he himself was responsible for building up. From that point on I think he has been convinced that, aside from brush wars, his real tool today, his real weapon, is the economic side of things rather than the military side. That being so, the logical question is, what are we doing about it? Are we to continue believing that we can separate our foreign policies from our trade policies. Somehow we content ourselves into believing that we can reach our objectives by doing this, just as we did in earlier years and just as the British empire used this policy down through the years
Therefore I am convinced, Mr. Chairman, that the basic premise which the minister attempted to lay before us this morning is wrong. While many of the arguments which he built upon that premise were reasonable- and certainly he has given a great deal of thought and effort to developing these-he can never expect to reach the goal which we know we must reach if we are to survive as a free nation in a free world. The minister said, "If only the communists in southeast Asia will give up their military subversion". Well, they will not do this; they will never do it. In fact they intend to step it up, because what they expect to do is take over southeast Asia. I believe there are only two alternatives for that troubled part of the world, and it is a critical part of the world today. Either there will be an all out conventional war, or southeast Asia will be lost altogether. How can neutrality further our purpose? In fact, I do not think the communists ever use the position of neutrality or agree to go along with it unless it is part of their specific strategy. When it no longer works to their advantage, they throw it aside. This is what has happened in Viet Nam; this is what has happened in Laos. And we


see, even with our peace keeping missions,, when the communists reach the point where they realize that neutrality is no longer furthering their objective, they withdraw their member altogether. This fact itself ought to speak very clearly to us. The peace keeping mission, as we heard in the news yesterday and today, and again in the statement made to us, have been able to keep their pledge of inspection on the neutral, or western, side but when they step across to the communist side, they cannot do it; it is impossible; it is not permitted.
I believe, also, that in this regard the minister overlooked a basic and very important factor on the international scene. This concerns President de Gaulle of France. It is obvious that he is determined to undermine the United States position wherever he can. In fact his obvious dislike of Americanism, and Anglo-Saxonism as well, indicates that he will resort even to using the communists to further his own objectives. This is rather clear in what has happened in Brazil in only the last few weeks. Here we find that he was giving at least encouragement of support to the Goulart administration. I think if what has happened there had not happened when it did, we probably would have had a communist coup before this date. De Gaulle lost out in his plans to use Brazil, and so now he is working against the American influence in southeast Asia. Any attempt to neutralize southeast Asia can result in nothing more or less than the loss of that entire area to the communists. By neutralization all we will do is help the communists reach their objective. His own ideas have become an obsession with him. That is why he has all but torpedoed NATO at the present time; that is why he was determined to prevent Great Britain from entering the European common market.
There is another omission which the minister has made in outlining government policy today. I do not think he did it intentionally. Perhaps in endeavouring to provide answers to some of these acute problems in crisis areas he merely overlooked it. This concerns the cold war, which seems to have become less of a military war and more of an economic war. The communist countries are in trouble and are not able to produce what they need. Therefore they come to us in their extremity and we help them out. Their system is unable to produce, unable even to meet the needs of their people for food. What we are doing in our present trade policies is assisting them in their weakness. Not only the commodities we sell to them but also the longer

term financing which we make available helps them to bridge over their problems. Russia could never be doing what she is doing in Egypt today, or in Algeria or other parts of the world, if she had to use all her efforts in meeting the problems in her own country. In this sense we are actually furthering the [DOT]aim of the Russians to bring about a communist state throughout the world.
I come now to the greatest omission of all made by the minister this morning. He did not even mention the underdeveloped nations as such. He mentioned southeast Asia, an area-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would my hon. friend forgive me. I mentioned that I had taken an hour and 20 minutes, but that I did propose at some point to discuss a number of problems, among them external aid. I would not want my hon. friend, who is very fair in these matters, to have the impression that the government is not interested in this- because it is.

I understand that the minister's time was limited and that is why I prefaced my statement by saying that he had probably overlooked it. But at this point it comes into the argument I am trying to develop, which is that we are attempting to carry our share of the load in the crisis areas of the world. I am thinking of the United Nations, NATO, southeast Asia and Cyprus. We are doing a commendable job, but are failing to take what is probably the greatest opportunity of all, and that is to help some of the uncommitted nations to develop to the point where they can look for their needs in light of what we understand and believe to be a free way of life.
I am thinking now particularly of the organization of African unity. There has been a tremendous revolution take place in Africa in recent years, some of it without bloodshed, some with. Unfortunately we learn of this through news media which emphasize only the violent aspect. I think one of the greatest opportunities before Canada is to understand what is taking place and to show those people that we are willing to carry our share of the load in helping them reach their goal. I think we should have permanent observers at the organization of African unity and should have direct diplomatic missions in more African countries. In this regard we ought to be stepping up our external aid program. It is not good enough to say that we are going to double it and let it go at that. I am convinced-I say this will all sincerity because I know the tremendous load the minister has in other parts of the
Supply*-External Affairs world-that perhaps an associate minister is required who could concentrate on the undeveloped areas of the world. He could go out carrying Canada's message to the countries of South America, of the Caribbean area as well as parts of the Far East and Africa. If such an additional position were created within the Department of External Affairs a tremendous amount of good would be accomplished which at the present time is not accomplished, simply because the burden of organization rests upon one person who cannot give the necessary attention to this very important aspect.
I mentioned the organization of African unity. We are all aware that there has been great bloodshed in the country of Rwanda. We are fearful what might happen in the Congo once the United Nations operation ceases. We know there is trouble in upper Sudan. We know there is trouble between Ethiopia and Somalia. We think also of countries like Algeria, Angola, Mozambique and central Africa. It is a fact that the African states themselves are making a real attempt to work out these problems in some kind of peaceful way. Then we read that Russia is moving in; that China is also moving into these areas and exercising a great deal of influence.
This also applies to the organization of American states. We hear a great deal about it not being advisable for Canada to become too closely related to problems in the southern hemisphere. On the other hand, how can we expect to be neighbours and convince them the way of life which we have in Canada with our free enterprise approach to living and the guarantee of those liberties which permit people to develop their initiative and have privileges which we sometimes regard all too lightly is the right way if we do not reach out to them as well?
Then there is the Caribbean area, quite apart from the American states. I do not think there is a person in the house this afternoon who would not agree that we should not do more to help our friends in the Caribbean get on their feet. There are small territories there which are isolated. The colonial office really has no longer any affection for them. The West Indies federation has collapsed. They need to be assisted and guided as they come closer to a new eastern Caribbean association. We are able to help them, and here lies a great opportunity.
We have a tremendous moral obligation in Canada which we are not fulfilling as we should. That is why I believe it would be

Supply-External Affairs a very practical suggestion that some provision be made in the Department of External Affairs to appoint an associate minister or some senior official who could truly represent Canada with the necessary prestige and authority, and who could concentrate on this important field.
I believe the minister was right when he said, in speaking about Berlin, that Berlin was the core of the European problem. I think what the minister should have done is to extend this illustration of Berlin to the whole picture in Europe. The problem NATO faces in Europe today will never be solved unless it is brought back to the point where the problem started. The problem NATO is facing in Europe today, with which we in the western world are so vitally concerned, begins with the very division of Europe. You cannot eliminate the disease unless you get to the root cause. I am sure the parliamentary secretary to the minister understands this even better than some of the rest of us. As far as Europe is concerned we must get back to the point that the only way to solve the problem is the reunification of Europe. I doubt whether there is one example the minister can cite where it can be proved that the communists ever carried out any commitment or agreement they had made, and did so in a way which fulfilled their obligation. As I was speaking about this to a friend, there arose the illustration of Austria. In my opinion Austria might be used as an example. I am convinced that the Russians were willing to go along with Austria in the way they did simply because it assisted them out of a very difficult situation. As they saw that western Austria was being used as one of the main transportation routes for supplies going into NATO, they were willing to withdraw if western Europe would also withdraw. They certainly removed a very difficult situation from their own hands and put it in NATO's lap.
The point I want to make here is that in dealing with the communist problem as it relates to NATO, let us face facts as they are. The minister stated this morning that we have to deal with the communists and have to work out ways of continuing peaceful negotiations, but on the other hand we must maintain our strength in order to carry out our obligations. In this connection I wonder if what NATO needs now is a new joint high command that would bring the various policies of NATO together, not just so far as the branches of the military forces are concerned, but to bring the various problems together, with someone in command of each

section. I am thinking of the political responsibility, the economic responsibility-yes, even the psychological aspect of it.
If NATO is to perform its real function in the years ahead, it cannot be regarded just as a military alliance. Certainly I agree with the minister when he says Canada is determined that it must be a trans-Atlantic organization, but, unless we bring all the aspects and phases of the problem together, and coordinate them under one main policy, NATO will not fulfil its obligation and do what it expected it to do.
When I suggest a joint high command, I am saying that we should have a specific department of NATO in each of these four fields, and then have over them a co-ordinated policy that will bring them together. At the present time Canada is strengthening its forces in NATO. I understand that Canada is not intending to increase its forces, though, when we heard the minister mention this morning that there are 25,000 Canadians in Germany, we fully realize that is not a small effort. Of course we must remember that this includes dependants and all the auxiliaries that go along with the military.
Yesterday in a newspaper report we were told about the re-equipping of our Canadian forces in NATO, and that the Honest John missiles are going to have nuclear warheads. But in another article in the same newspaper I read that, though France is withdrawing from NATO, she intends to bring back into it a ground to ground missile far superior to the Honest John. In view of the tremendous development of West Germany, the recovery of France and Italy, and the development of some other NATO powers, I question if it is essential for us to continue keeping such a large NATO contingent, in the military sense.
If NATO is to continue in a positive role it needs to be reorganized along the lines I have previously mentioned, and Canada should play a far greater part in the economic and psychological aspect than she does in the military aspect.
Referring briefly to Cyprus. This is indeed a difficult problem. Actually, it brings us back to the United Nations at this time and, more specifically, to the visit of the secretary general of the United Nations. In last night's Montreal Star there was a very timely article in regard to the visit of U Thant to Ottawa, and I would like to place one or two paragraphs from it on the record:
For their part, Canadians will be able to assess a secretary general who has called upon Canada to assume an increasingly heavy UN burden in terms of men and money for UN operations.

However, If anything concrete is to come from the Thant visit, it will be incumbent upon the secretary general to clarify for Canadians just what role Canada is to play in a UN that has changed radically in the last five years.
Since assuming power, the secretary general has followed the Hammarskjold tradition by playing up to the newly emerging nations of Africa and Asia.
It must remembered that Canada is just one of 112 members of the United Nations and I think the secretary general should be reminded, though no doubt he is well informed about it, that we contributed something more than $20 million to United Nations operations in the last year, and that this does not include some of the peace keeping operations which we have paid for directly. Out of a total budget of some $300 million we contributed that much, when actually we represent, so far as voting power is concerned, only one one hundred and twelfth.
The visit of the secretary general to Ottawa is a significant one because it brings us to the question of how long we are to continue these peace keeping missions through the United Nations and still have the same lack of cooperation from other members of the organization. Specifically at the moment this concerns the Cyprus operation. Yes, we are carrying our share. We are doing our best. We are helping to settle the hot spots. We are playing a leading role in setting up within our armed forces a special unit available at all times to assist in peace keeping. This is good; but we must understand that beyond all this there is a greater responsibility.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, I would like to mention the commonwealth. I believe we speak and think too little about the commonwealth, and the important part it can play. Somehow we think about it as something of the past, but the commonwealth of today represents some 700 million people, and is one of the greatest vehicles we could use to discharge the responsibility of helping the underdeveloped nations of the world.
The commonwealth education conference is to be held this year in Ottawa. It would be good for the minister to consider, in addition to the regular agenda, the arranging for a study period for those delegates who are coming from underdeveloped areas. It could last for a month, or possibly two or three months. I personally have had letters from a number of delegates whom I know, asking if they could not stay here for a couple of months in order to study the Canadian educational system, to take a short course that would help them when they return to their own countries. Again this is the kind of thing
Supply-External Affairs that we can do in Canada and which does not cost a lot of money.
In closing may I say, let us not think in Canada that we are a great military force which can compete with the great nations of the world such as the United States, the U.S.S.R., France, and Great Britain. We cannot do that. Any attempt to try and imitate them is just going to frustrate and confuse the picture so far as our own responsibilities and obligations are concerned. We are in a peculiar situation. Formerly we were a colony, but have reached our own independence. We have developed on a free basis a tremendous economy that rates high among the other nations of the world. We have a tremendous reserve of good will in the world. These things should all be tied together in our external affairs policy, in our defence policy, and in our politics as they relate to the international scene. They should all be co-ordinated so that we can make a greater contribution for world peace.
Again, coming back to the very fundamental need across the world, which is in two words, perhaps more vitally and clearly to the people of the underdeveloped countries than in any other words: world hunger. If we can align our policies and set our actions in a direction that will assist people in these countries meet their needs more effectively, then we can make the greatest contribution to the world scene, and accomplish much more than we are doing at present.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. member would answer a question. I did not want to interrupt him during his remarks. Does he still take the position that he and his group are against selling western wheat to Russia and China?
Well-
Let me finish. Is he still against that and, if not, what is his policy in that regard and why has he changed?
If the hon. member for Bow valley-
Bow River is my constituency.

-has not found the answer to his question from the remarks I have made, then he is not able to understand very well what I have been saying. But I will be very specific. He just loves to stand up and say to the people of western Canada that I am against selling the farmers' wheat. What I am interested in doing, Mr. Chairman, is assisting the people of the underdeveloped nations with the tremendous reserves of food

Supply-External Affairs products we have in this country and with the know-how that is behind them in a way that we can strengthen them in their stand in wanting to be part of the free world. If we subvert our trade policies to anything else I think we are not accomplishing what we should.
I wonder whether the hon. member would answer one more question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Perhaps I should mention to the committee that the hon. member's time has expired, but if it is the unanimous wish of the committee a question might be asked. The hon. member for Chapleau.
I will be brief.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed the hon. member may ask a question?
Agreed.

We all agree with regard to feeding the people of the underdeveloped nations, but my question was a direct one and the hon. member for Red Deer said he would give a direct answer. Is he against trading with red China and Russia in western wheat?
The hon. member for Bow valley-
Bow River is my constituency.

Bow River-is very concerned about this problem. What I have said time and again I will say to him now. I believe our policies should be directed in a way that we can sell our wheat to our friends instead of to those who are threatening to destroy the very way of life that we regard as right. Until these policies can be worked out and some of the economic problems involved in them can also be resolved, not to sell our wheat would certainly be utter folly. I have never said anything other than that, but I believe we have a far greater obligation to our neighbours and friends than we have to others who may be on the other side of the world, and on the other side of the fence.

This morning, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), in his splendid statement, took us around the world. In my estimation, he did not take up too much of our time, since his activities have led him everywhere in the world. This is a part of his duties, and he showed us to some extent what is happening in the world. It was quite proper that the minister should

report on his work, his observations, and the stand he took to influence, as it were, the nations with whom he discussed for peace.
I would like to point out immediately to the minister and the members of the house that I agree with those who believe that we must discuss with the other countries in the world and organize cultural and trade exchanges with foreign countries in order to obtain a durable peace.
I believe that this dialogue tending to obtain better understanding and more comprehension between the countries of the world is necessary. I also believe that we, Canadians, are to a certain extent willing and ready to help underdeveloped countries to get their economy going and to teach them to help themselves.
However, I wonder whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs was well equipped during his meetings to offer those countries the solutions they need. It is all right to go to your neighbour offering to help him tidy up his home, but, Mr. Chairman, I believe that one should first tidy up one's own place.
I am not convinced that real peace is prevailing at home. I know that the minister is aware of the great amount of distress to be found all over the world, and of the poverty prevailing in too many countries, and I admit that they should be enabled to shake off this state of destitution. I also agree that there are in this world, and in our own country as everywhere else, ever increasing and more extensive means to help those countries fight the destitution found all over the world, so that it should not get a permanent hold in spite of the new scientific and technical developments, in spite of the machines and automation, that are, or should be, at our disposal.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I believe that in order to be well equipped to offer those countries efficient solutions, it would be in order to look and observe at home, in the four corners of the country, with a view to discovering whether we are not also somewhat underdeveloped.
Not very long ago it was reported that we could number in this country 35 designated areas where depression still prevails. There are 35 underdeveloped areas which encompass not only a city or a village; each of them represents quite a considerable area.
Well, under the circumstances, I wonder whether we are justified in trying to clean up our neighbour's house.

Solutions are being offered and should be implemented. On the other hand, I shall have later on an opportunity to come back to this subject. But in the meantime I would like to ask the minister for some explanation, for instance, in regard to the United Nations.
According to the news we get and which comes from reliable sources, it seems that the member countries of the UN have not quite honoured their obligations or met their commitments toward that organization. In fact, it appears that Canada is the most generous country and also the most aware of its obligations. Therefore, I think that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should clear up that matter by telling us what is the total amount of all the contributions owed to the UN and how many countries have not yet paid theirs? Besides, he could tell us whether, in his opinion, those commitments will soon be fulfilled.
Mr. Chairman, as far as I am concerned, I have some doubts about the results of the action of the United Nations force in Cyprus. This is a personal opinion, based on what I saw or what I learned from reports published in the large newspapers from other countries. My doubts are based on the results obtained by the United Nations forces in other countries faced with domestic difficulties.
As an example, I should like to mention the case of Korea where soldiers from various countries were implicated. Did that action prevent the destruction of that country? I think not.
And more recently, Canada sent troops to the Congo, and there again, one may wonder if our interference prevented trouble or disturbances. On the contrary, we heard that murders had been committed, that disasters, engagements and even assassinations had taken place, in spite of the presence of United Nations forces.
Mr. Chairman, those are the reasons why I feel justified to wonder whether the results which our soldiers will obtain in Cyprus will be any better than in the past. At least, I hope so, since we have become involved.
During his statement the minister referred to the fear now existing in the free world facing communism and its threats. I think that communism, whether it comes from white Russia or yellow China is no less a red communism, and it is dangerous, wherever it comes from. But we do not simply have to face up to communism. If communism, where it has taken root, did not succeed in achieving its objective, that is in ensuring security, it did succeed nevertheless in depriving the people of freedom, without ensuring the se-20220-223
Supply-External Affairs curity it had promised. Nevertheless, those countries are suffering from poverty and insecurity.
On the other hand, there is another group which is no less dangerous and which rules the world, at least in part. I refer to free masonry, an anti-Christian and anti-religious society which has kept the world and the working class in dire poverty since it came into existence. Communism is also an antireligious and anti-Christian society which has achieved the same objectives.
Mr. Chairman, those organizations have given us and are maintaining a false system. In spite of the abundance which exists, they are keeping the world and its peoples in the most abject and intolerable poverty. Such poverty is due to an organization and a system which are false.
That system exists not only in what we call the old countries, those of old Europe, Asia or anywhere you please, but here also: even if Canada is a comparatively young country, we have copied a little the old methods of those countries.
Mr. Chairman, those systems breed poverty and keep the people in that intolerable poverty.
A few years ago a former leader of the Conservative party, who was then premier of Manitoba-I mean Hon. John Bracken-stated at a federal-provincial conference in 1941:
Under the present tax system the income of the relatively poor is transferred to the relatively rich.
That tax system, Mr. Chairman, is forced upon us by a debt-money system which does not take into account the country's economic realities or its production capacity. That tax system which was already bad in 1941 and even before-but that premier recognized it in 1941-and which transfers the income of the relatively poor to the relatively rich, is still with us. This is where some changes are needed if we want to be able to show the other countries of the world that it is possible to fight poverty and give each person in those countries, as well as in our own, a purpose in life and the proper means to achieve it.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock? [Text]
