subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-35, to amend the Criminal Code (habeas corpus).
He said: In rising to speak on this Bill C-35 I should like to tell hon. members that this is the same bill as Bill No. C-77, read on November 12, 1962, for the first time and the same as Bill C-42, read on May 20, 1963, for the first time. So this is the third time that this amendment to the Criminal Code has been spoken to.
This is a very simple amendment, when one looks at the words actually involved. The proposal is to add three words to section 691 of the Criminal Code, the words "or habeas corpus".
This is the result of a recommendation to me from a distinguished friend, Professor H. R. S. Ryan, Q.C., who is known to a good many members of the house, now a professor of law at Queen's University law school, a man who prior to teaching law spent many years as a successful counsel. He is also one of our best known students of penology. It was Mr. Ryan's suggestion, in a letter to me on November 5, 1962, that this bill should be produced. I was supported in the preparation of this measure by advice from an old teacher of mine, a man young in years but long in experience of criminal law, Mr. G. Arthur Martin, Q.C. Mr. Martin wrote me on December 7, 1962, saying:
I think that the lack of appeal in habeas corpus proceedings constituted a gap in the law which the proposed amendment remedies.
I have also discussed this matter with Mr. John Robinette, Q.C. and Mr. Royden Hughes, Q.C. who are well known in criminal law circles. There is, however, nothing new in this recommendation, which is an attempt to implement a suggestion made by Chief Justice McRuer of the high court of Ontario in the case known as "Re Shane".
Before discussing this case may I say, for the benefit of lay colleagues in the house, that habeas corpus is one of the most ancient and honoured of the writs known to English law. In the most recent copy of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, the author says on this subject:
From the earliest records of the English law no free man could be detained in custody except on a criminal charge or conviction or for a civil debt. It is granted only on application to the high court or a judge thereof, supported by a sworn statement of facts setting up at least a probable case of illegal confinement. It is addressed to the person in whose custody another is detained,
[The Chairman.]
and commands him to bring his prisoner before the court immediately after the receipt of the writ.
Halsbury, in his Laws of England, the third edition, volume II described it as being-
-a prerogative writ by which the Queen has a right to inquire into the causes for which any of her subjects are deprived of their liberty. By it the high court and the judges of that court, at the instance of a subject aggrieved, command the production of that subject, and inquire into the cause of his imprisonment. If there is no legal justification for the detention, the party is ordered to be released.
It is, of course, further pointed out:
Release on habeas corpus is not, however, an acquittal, nor may the writ be used as a means of appeal.
Hon. members may inquire as to the timeliness of bringing forward a bill making provision for the right of appeal in connection with habeas corpus. I think that all over Canada we are concerned, today, with civil liberties and the rights of individuals. I have here a clipping from the Brockville Recorder and Times of November 26, 1964 where the writer of an editorial on civil liberties asks this question: "What happened to Gerard Bigras, 29, of Sudbury, who was sentenced to seven days in jail and 83 days later was still in jail?" The article continues:
This points up a glaring weakness in our system of law, when a man can be stuck in jail and nearly forgotten.
We all know that Chief Justice McRuer has served Canada in various capacities as counsel, prosecutor, chairman of various important royal commissions and, of course, as chief justice of the high court of Ontario. The learned chief justice in the Shane case looked very carefully at the legal authorities. Perhaps I may read briefly from the head-note. The headnote to "Re Shane" which is reported in 19 D.L.R., second edition, and at page 460 reads as follows-the hearing took place on May 20, 1959:
A prisoner has no right of appeal from an order of a judge of the supreme court (Ont.) refusing a discharge under habeas corpus proceedings and neither can he apply from judge to judge of that court until he obtains a decision in his favour or until all judges (31 in all) have heard his application. Once his application for discharge has been refused that is an end of the matter and semble, it makes no difference that, as here, the prisoner is held under the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 322. The present situation, which places the liberty of the subject in the hands of one individual judge, can only be remedied by legislative action providing for a right of appeal in habeas corpus matters.
The learned chief justice had this to say, as reported at page 465 of the reports:

In disposing of the case I respectfully suggest that prompt action should be taken by proper authorities to resolve the confusion that now exists and to provide for the right of appeal in habeas corpus matters that was thought to exist prior to the decision of the Court of Appeal in this case.
I might indicate to hon. members that Professor Ryan has drawn to my attention the fact that the conference of commissioners on criminal legislation has recommended at least once-in the year 1959-that provision for an appeal be restored to section 691.1 beg to point out, also, that this matter has been considered by courts of appeal in other provinces. One of the important cases is "In Re Fred Storgoff" reported on page 526 of S.C.R., 1945 where it was found that the federal government had exclusive jurisdiction to authorize such an appeal under the provisions of the British North America Act, sections 91(27) and 92(13). In this case there was reference to the dictum of Lord Halsbury who said:
For a period extending as far back as our legal history the writ of habeas corpus has been regarded as one of the most important safeguards of the liberty of the subject.
Lord Birkenhead is recorded to have said:
We are dealing with a writ antecedent to statute, and throwing its roots deep into the genius of our common law. It is perhaps the most important writ known to the constitutional law of England, affording as it does a swift and imperative remedy in all cases of illegal restraint or confinement. It is of immemorial antiquity, an instance of its use occurring in the thirty third year of Edward I. It has through the ages been jealously maintained by courts of law as a check upon the illegal usurpation of power by the executive at the cost of the liege.
Finally, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, C.J.C., who was a well known Quebecker, said application for this writ was "unquestionably the first security of civil liberty". The same ideas are contained in the case of Wattebled v. Lesage and Aubut and attorney general of the province, as reported at page 108 of C.B.R., 1953. Here we find a dictum of Mr. Justice Tasche-reau. He points out that this ancient writ-
-dates back farther than the Magna Carta of Jean Sans-Terre, it was jus non scrivtum. and it was only in 1679 that it appeared in the statutes of England.
This was "an act for the better securing the liberty of the subject and for the prevention of imprisonment beyond the seas".
In some circumstances appeal has not been provided for in our code. The failure to provide appeal in habeas corpus was, I think, inadvertent. This gap in judicial remedy has been recognized by those jurists who make periodic examination of our code, and I believe they have recommended from time 20220-2234
Criminal Code
to time to the Department of Justice that this oversight be corrected.
I shall not trespass further on the time of the house. I simply indicate that this bill is an attempt to do what has been recommended by His Lordship Chief Justice McRuer in Re Shane and follows logically from the conclusions of other important judgments that have been given by the courts of appeal of various provinces and the Supreme Court of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) for bringing forward this bill. I might say at the outset that I am going to support it without any reservation or equivocation whatsoever. I will try to be as brief as I can because I know the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), and perhaps other hon. members, will want to speak on this matter. Also, I do not want to take up too much time, in order that perhaps this matter can be dealt with and the bill passed today.
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, we are considering one of our special, extraordinary remedies that deals with the rights of an individual. We are dealing with habeas corpus, of course, and we are dealing with that kind of right which is afforded a person in custody. There are many extraordinary remedies; there is the right of habeas corpus, certiorari, mandamus, and others. But in this case we are dealing with habeas corpus, which is very important because we are dealing with the right of a person to make an application for release when he is held illegally in custody, This situation arises when an inferior court, by its judgment, has placed someone in custody and has either exceeded its jurisdiction, exceeded the law, or the decision is against the natural law of justice. It is one of those rights which we have that protects the individual and guarantees his freedom in this country under the rule of law as we know it. After all, our democratic processes are based on the rule of law and not on the rule of people.
What is the law at the present time? It may be that there has been more litigation in this country in reference to habeas corpus than with regard to any other facet or phase of criminal law. I am going to refer to various cases briefly, just to place them on the record; not particularly to emphasize the facts but just to give a portion of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada. I did not have too long to prepare these remarks this afternoon. I knew this bill was

Criminal Code
coming before the house, but some of the other bills were stood.
One of the earliest cases is Smith v. The King, 1931 S.C.R., at page 531. Another case is In Re Jack Goldhar, 1958 S.C.R., at page 693. There is also another decision on the same case by the whole court, reported in 1960 S.C.R. at page 435. I might just pause there, Mr. Speaker, and say that the 1958 case was a decision of Mr. Justice Martland sitting in chambers and the decision in 1960 was by the supreme court on the same set of facts. Then there is the case of Re Shane, which has been referred to by the hon. member for Leeds. That case is reported in 19 D.L.R. (2d) at page 460. Then there is the case of In Re Storgoff, 1945 S.C.R., page 527.
What is the law when one reads these cases? Before referring to that question, Mr. Speaker, I might just say that at one time it was the feeling, when someone was making an application because he felt his liberty had been usurped by being held in custody, that you could apply to a judge of any superior court in the trial division, any judge of the court of appeal, and then you could apply to a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada; but it was finally decided that you could go to only one judge in one court, and having done that your remedy, as I understand the law, is at an end. In other words, the law today is that if one is held on a charge under the Criminal Code of Canada-I emphasize the Criminal Code of Canada because we have to differentiate between offences under the common law and those under the Criminal Code, and I will have something to say about that in a few moments-you could go to any one judge; you can go to a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or, in my province, which happens to be where I practise law, you can go to a judge of the trial division of Alberta, or a judge of the appellate division, which is our court of appeal in Alberta. This applies to any province.
The next question is this. On the statute books of each province there is some statutory law, or there are some rules which are codified by the legislature of the province, which allow you to go to the court of appeal only on matters with regard to which the province has jurisdiction. For example, there is the dental act, and if someone was found guilty of malpractice on summary conviction and the magistrate or board had exceeded their jurisdiction under that act, you could go to a trial judge and then to the court of appeal of Alberta. This is true in

regard to the various provinces, I believe. I know it is true in British Columbia and Alberta.
The next point is this. Until April 1, 1955 there was a differentiation as between an offence under the common law of Canada and one under the Code of Canada. Now, since the new amendment, those offences are all under the Criminal Code of Canada and there is no differentiation between offences which are under the common law and those which are under the Code. At one time a person who was charged with an offence under the common law of Canada, but not under the Code, could not apply for habeas corpus; it did not apply in his case. In particular, he did not have the right to go to the Supreme Court of Canada. He may, of course, have had the right to go to a judge in his own jurisdiction.
Let us look for a few moments at these authorities. The first case I mentioned was the famous Smith case. It is Art J. Smith v. The King. The appellant in this case bears no relationship to the famous Arthur Smith who was a Queen's Counsel in Alberta, or his son. A different set of facts are involved, and a different province. This case states:
The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada in respect of habeas corpus extends only to cases of commitment following upon charges of offences which are criminal by virtue of statutes enacted by the parliament of Canada-
That is what I was saying; the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada applied only to those offences under the Code and not to those under the common law. Since the amendments to the Code of April 1, 1955, any offences under the common law are now part of the Criminal Code in this regard and therefore there is jurisdiction in this respect.
The next case I referred to was In Re Jack Goldhar which, as I said, came before Mr. Justice Martland in chambers. Mr. Justice Martland was a judge of our Supreme Court of Canada. He said that as it was no longer possible to prosecute a person for an offence at common law, there could no longer be a commitment in a criminal case for such an offence, and any offence thereafter charged under the Criminal Code must be considered as a criminal case under an act of the parliament of Canada. Therefore the Supreme Court of Canada would have jurisdiction under the Code and under the common law, because the common law had now been codified. That decision was appealed; the decision of one judge of the Supreme Court of Canada was appealed to the whole court, and that decision was upheld. The judgment

was written by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada at that time.
Dealing with the Shane case, this is the problem-and I am going to come to grips with it. The problem is that at the present time you can only get this remedy from one judge at a time. You can go only to one judge. At one time there was a lot of law to the effect that you could move from one judge to another. At the present time the law seems to be very firm that you can go to one judge in the superior court, but there is no right of appeal. You have to distinguish between a civil remedy and a criminal remedy. That is because we have quasi-criminal offences.
Let me give an example, Mr. Speaker, of a case I had myself concerning a dispute between the dentists of the province of Alberta and the dental mechanics. Charges were laid against the dental mechanics of manufacturing teeth. They were quasi-criminal charges. If a mistake were made in law by a magistrate or an inferior court, then you had the remedy of habeas corpus if the accused were in custody, or if not in custody, on certiorari, to go for trial in the province. Then there was an appeal to the court of appeal of Alberta. The same procedure existed in the province of British Columbia. Unfortunately, under the offences in the Criminal Code of Canada there does not seem to be an appeal provided for to the courts of appeal of the provinces, as established by the Re Shane case. I discussed this question privately with the hon. member for Leeds a few minutes before five o'clock, and under his bill which he has presented today to the house provision will be made only for an appeal to the court of appeal of a province. I do not think that anyone would like to see, unless a mistake in law had been made, all of these matters go to the Supreme Court of Canada. But I think it is a good thing that we should at least have a right of appeal to the appeal courts in the respective provinces which have jurisdiction as far as the Criminal Code is concerned.
In that regard this bill is a necessary amendment, because if a trial judge does make a mistake, or if he does not agree with the applicant's counsel, the applicant can at least have the decision of the judge reviewed by five judges of the provincial court of appeal. That is true in any criminal matter if you lose a decision before a judge or are convicted before a jury. In Alberta, which is the only province where you can have a case before the supreme court trial division
Criminal Code
without a jury, if the trial judge has made a mistake in any criminal matter you can appeal on a question of law or on a question of fact in law to the court of appeal. This amendment would mean that if a decision on a question of habeas corpus is unfavourable to the applicant he can have it reviewed by the court of appeal of the province. In that regard I congratulate the hon. member for Leeds for bringing forth this amendment, and I hope it passes.
In dealing with the extraordinary remedies, I think there is one thought which parliament should have, as we sit here passing legislation in this house. I can spend the rest of my time talking about various examples, where, by statute, is taken away the right of habeas corpus and the right of certiorari, which are extraordinary remedies and protect the individual against the infringement of the state where the law is exceeded.
In this regard we need only look at the Income Tax Act, which is a terrible act in this regard. It is only under very unusual circumstances that you can apply this extraordinary remedy. We have only to look at provincial statutes and at our archaic liquor laws. Provincial legislation always makes me laugh. We are always so holy in this country with reference to our liquor laws, while the provincial treasurers take into their accounts about $6 million each year. Yet under those acts it seems to be legal to sell liquor but illegal to drink liquor in most places. In these particular statutes-and this is the point I am making-you will read time and time again that there is taken away the right of habeas corpus and the right of certiorari. They want to make it so tough for the accused that if he is ever charged under the liquor acts he cannot help but get fined or imprisoned. If the law has been exceeded then you have not the extraordinary remedies which you have in normal cases under the Criminal Code and other statutes.
So I say in passing that I endorse this amendment; but I suggest to any future parliament-and I hope the legislators follow suit-that when we are shaping legislation with reference to penal matters we do not take away these extraordinary remedies, because in many cases under the federal Income Tax Act and under the provincial liquor acts injustices are done to individuals. Sometimes they are held in custody illegally. They are fined or their books are seized illegally. These extraordinary remedies which exist in other phases of our law should exist as far as those statutes are concerned. Particularly

Criminal Code
in provinces where the revenue from the sale of liquor is sizeable the legislators could certainly leave the law the same as it was under the common law as it exists under the Criminal Code. Because if a provincial statute is to become a penal statute, then why have you not all of the remedies which exist under the offences described in the Code?
So I say in summary, realizing that others want to speak, that this is a good suggestion because the application can be made only to one judge of the court. If that judge makes a mistake in reviewing the record of an inferior court as far as the extraordinary remedies of habeas corpus or certiorari are concerned, you have a right of appeal to the court of appeal of the province. We have that right now in quasi-criminal matters or in civil matters, such as the case of the dentists where the dental mechanics were charged with making teeth, because it was alleged they were practising dentistry. We considered the magistrate in that case exceeded his jurisdiction. We considered another board which dealt with the dentists also exceeded their jurisdiction in that regard. You have a right of appeal in these matters in Alberta. In criminal matters, whatever the charge is, whether it be serious or is another offence under the Code, where habeas corpus applies, when an accused is in custody, or certiorari applies where he is not in custody, there is the right of review by the top court of appeal in the province. Since April 1, 1955 we have taken steps to see that all matters are now dealt with as if they come under the Code.
This is another step in the history of jurisprudence of this country and I endorse the bill entirely. I congratulate the hon. member for Leeds for presenting it, and I trust that when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) speaks he will support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that this bill should be passed should become very obvious to us all when we realize that the lawyers and members of this house, who usually agree about little or nothing, are all agreed that it is a good bill and that it should be passed. I think the best contribution I can make toward passing this bill is to confine my remarks to a very few minutes of time, and I will certainly do that.
I should just like to point out to any hon. member not aware of it that what the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) has described in the remedy of habeas corpus as an ancient and honourable remedy-I think he used those words-is the fundamental means

whereby the rule of law and the liberty
of the subject have been worked out and preserved during centuries of history. This is one of the great achievements of our system. The security of every individual person against arbitrary imprisonment is based upon this remedy of habeas corpus.
This bill which is recommended to us not only by the words of the hon. member who spoke with obviously good sense, but also by a very distinguished justice, Chief Justice McRuer-who happened to be my partner once, although I did not agree with him in everything-gives the right of appeal where some judge has refused this remedy to effectuate the liberty of the subject.
For myself, I have had enough experience with courts to have learned that judges are not infallible. They are human, and they perform better sometimes if their acts are subject to review by higher courts. I think this is a very commendable thing. I am not going to elaborate on the learning put before the house by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), which I found very interesting. I just wish to commend the bill to the house and to commend the honourable, learned and distinguished member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) for having introduced it into the house.

Mr. Speaker, I do not lay any great claim to an understanding of legal terminology or practice, but it seems to me that the amendment proposed this afternoon is one that commends itself to the principles of humanity and justice.
Before taking part in this debate I asked the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) if it would be permissible for me, a layman, to enter a debate such as this, and he gave his consent. Possibly it is a case of a layman moving in where angels fear to tread. I assure the house, however, that I am not going to enter deeply into the discussion that is taking place.
It has been indicated that this is an amendment which has the support of many of those who are well versed in legal matters. It has been recommended as a remedy for what appears to be an oversight or omission of the drafting of the present legislation. The fact that it has been supported by those in the legal profession, and has been so ably and conscientiously introduced by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), for whom I have the greatest respect and in whose judgment I have great confidence, prompts me to voice support for the amendment before us.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend wholeheartedly the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) and say that I fully support the bill he submitted to the house in order to preserve individual liberty, in conformity with the principles of the bill on human rights recently passed by this house.
I believe this is to reduce to the minimum any arbitrary imprisonment or denial of liberty, of an individual by providing for an appeal from the decision of a court having denied an application for a writ of habeas corpus.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to state briefly a very deplorable situation which exists in some of our Quebec criminal courts.
There we find a situation commonly known as "fixing". "Fixing" is a scheme by which one speculates on the sentences to be imposed, sentences which are prolonged or reduced according to the talkativeness or otherwise of an accused or an individual who confesses to the police.
Indeed, a despicable game is often played between lawyers, police officers and judges, who get together to speculate on the length of the detention period, based on whether the persons held in custody have satisfied or not the curiosity of certain police officers who do not care too much for the dignity of the human person. Those police officers often vent their bad temper on others by resorting to violence.
The Coffin investigation shows that there is something wrong with the administration of justice. A Montreal judge has requested a thorough investigation, and he is right. Judge Wagner asked for a thorough investigation of justice, and I feel that as the world fair is approaching, there will be a great promiscuity among people coming from all parts of the world, so there is reason to fear a new outbreak of criminality.

Criminal Code

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too appreciate the principle behind this bill. Habeas corpus, the English meaning of which is to have the body, is a direction by the court to the authorities to bring the body of a person-the live body, of course-of a person who is held in custody under confinement before the court, so that the authorities may justify their detention. I often think, after several years in this house, that when all else fails here we raise a point of privilege. When all else fails in court a person in jail raises a writ of habeas corpus.
May I just add one thing to what has been said. The case to which the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) made reference is one based on an English decision. Before that decision it had been impressed on most members of the legal fraternity that a solicitor or counsel for a man held in custody, if rejected by one judge, could then go from judge to judge and keep making his application for habeas corpus; but an English decision indicated that this was an incorrect assumption on the part of the law, the lawyers and the judges. Therefore this was followed by Chief Justice McRuer's action, with the effect mentioned.
However, I would point out that prior to that decision it had not been a wholly unsatisfactory state of affairs where, within reasonable limits, you might go to successive judges. I point that out for this reason. It may well happen that the confinement under which the accused person is being held might be of a limited nature. By the time you get to the court of appeal it might be too late. This accounts for the reason why, having been turned down by one judge in the morning, you go to another judge in the afternoon. There are obviously limits to the application of a principle of that kind, as Chief Justice McRuer pointed out. In the province of Ontario which has 36 judges, and probably more now, it would be an obvious abuse of the legal procedures.
But I would suggest to the Minister of Justice-while I hope he will give an indication that he is going to consent to the amendment at this time-that he might give consideration to including at some later time, in conjunction with it, a limited right which could be incorporated under section 424 of the

Criminal Code
Criminal Code, where there is given to courts of appeal the right to make recommendations on procedure. This is the section under which the various provincial courts have made recommendations on the procedure, under authority of the federal parliament, with regard to criminal matters. I suggest that the minister give the provincial courts of appeal the right, under section 424, and by a further amendment to section 691, to provide for limited access to individual judges, as well as the right of appeal.
I emphasize the reason for that in this fact that there are a number of cases which occur to my mind, and I think the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) illustrated this by reference to small penalties which might be imposed in respect of certain offences, and by the time you get into the court of appeal it is all over, and, while you might have the honour of the declaration by the court of appeal that you were unjustly imprisoned, that is not always a salutary remedy. I would suggest to the minister in conclusion that he might give some consideration to the suggestion I have made. All it would take would be a legislative enactment to restore the right which the legal profession considered did exist prior to the English decision followed by Chief Justice McRuer. It would permit in some provinces limited access to a number of trial judges of the superior court, which might be desirable. I would ask the minister to consider the possibility of some limited right of application to successive judges in certain cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take this unique opportunity to say that I agree not only with the spokesmen of my party, but also with all those of the opposition who have expressed their views. This is an opportunity that might not happen again very often in this house.
I am also happy to congratulate the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) on the civic sense and the understanding of the administration of justice in this country he has shown by introducing the bill now under consideration.
The situation he pointed out is one which constituted an anomaly up to now. Section 691 of the Criminal Code which is sought to be amended by the present bill, refers to three methods of examination or of statement of invalidity with regard to conviction or imprisonment.

I do not want to discuss here, in a technical way, those three methods, but they are mentioned in that section: mandamus, certiorari and prohibition. The only test of the legality of a conviction and the only means of getting directly out of jail the person who complains about the decision, is through the procedure of habeas corpus which was well explained before I rose. It is abnormal that the code should include at the present time a provision which, in the case of the other three procedures, stipulates the right of appeal but entirely omits to stipulate it in the case that is undoubtedly the most important of those privilege proceedings, that is habeas corpus.
As Minister of Justice, I must say that even if this bill is not a government bill I had that same amendment in mind. As a citizen, as a member of the Quebec bar, the Ontario bar and the Canadian bar, it is a measure I wanted to see introduced.
Indeed, I remember that during the last five or six years I was associated with the faculty of law of the University of Ottawa, one of the subjects I taught dealt precisely with those extraordinary writs called "prerogative writs". Every year, and especially since the appeal court's decision in the Storgoff case, to which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) referred, I would point out to my students this anomaly where an appeal could be heard on the other three writs but not on a writ of habeas corpus in a criminal case.
That is why I feel it is a duty for me to give full support to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Leeds. In my opinion, its passage would be a step forward in the administration of justice and I hope that the house will pass it.

I note in the explanatory notes, however, that it is five years since the suggestion was first made, so that it is not prejudicial in any manner to this bill to make reference to the law's interminable delays.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPEAL IN HABEAS CORPUS PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
The wording in the explanatory notes stating that "the present situation . . . places the liberty of the subject

in the hands of one individual judge" attracts my attention. I agree that there should be an appeal in such a situation and I am happy that the hon. member for Leeds has introduced this bill. I am very pleased to know that it has the approval of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). But as a layman and not a lawyer, and as one who never uses a thousand words where one will do, and who has never studied law, I should like to ask the Minister of Justice to give consideration, after this amendment is passed, to the fact that certain judges-I will not name any of them here, but most Ontario people know to whom I refer-make use of the power they have with regard to contempt of court in what I think is an improper way. There is certainly no appeal from the decision made by one judge in such a case, which lets the hammer of the law fall on the subject, and certainly the liberty of the subject is at the disposition of the judge.
I am thinking in particular of a friend of mine in the city of Cornwall in the riding represented by the Deputy Speaker who was subjected to a contempt of court decision by an authority I do not need to name. That means that the record of this decision will stand against him. I do not think the action of the judge in the case was correct at all. That man had no appeal from the decision of the judge; but now we have high authority quoted today to indicate that the circumstances covered by the bill place the liberty of the subject in the hands of one individual judge.
Business of the House
There is one judge of the Ontario high court who finds there has been contempt of court more frequently than all the other judges on that bench. I hope that the Minister of Justice, in approving of the amendment of the hon. member for Leeds, will give consideration to action to provide an appeal from the sentence of an individual judge in a contempt of court accusation.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.
